The Fall of the USSR
ЗАСТОЙ
1964 – 1985

Economic Stagnation

On the surface, the Soviet Union looked like a stable superpower. Underneath, its economy was slowing down and its people were losing faith.

What Happened?

Leonid Brezhnev (pictured) led the Soviet Union from 1964 until his death in 1982. His government valued stability above all else: party officials kept their jobs for decades, and few reforms were attempted. Later Soviet leaders would call this period the "Era of Stagnation."

The planned economy struggled to produce the consumer goods people wanted. Long lines for basic items like meat, shoes, and toilet paper became part of daily life, and a black market grew to fill the gaps. Meanwhile, the government spent a huge share of its budget on the military to keep pace with the United States in the Cold War.

  1. 1964

    Brezhnev takes power. He replaces Nikita Khrushchev and rolls back many of Khrushchev's reforms.

  2. 1972

    The USSR buys grain from the West. Soviet farms cannot feed the country, so the government begins importing millions of tons of grain from the United States and Canada.

  3. 1970s

    Oil money hides the problems. Rising world oil prices bring in cash from Soviet oil exports, covering up how poorly the rest of the economy is performing.

  4. 1982 – 1985

    Three leaders in three years. Brezhnev dies in 1982. His elderly successors, Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko, both die within months of each other.

Key Terms

Stagnationзастой
A period with little growth or change. Describes the Soviet economy and government under Brezhnev.
Planned economy
An economy where the government, not the market, decides what is produced, how much, and at what price.
Black market
Illegal buying and selling of goods, often things that are scarce or banned.

What Role Did It Play in the Collapse?

Stagnation was the slow-burning problem underneath every other crisis. The Soviet economy could not keep up with the West, and ordinary people could see it in the empty shelves and long lines. When world oil prices crashed in the mid-1980s, the money that had been hiding the problem dried up.

Stagnation also convinced Communist Party leaders that something had to change. That is why they chose a younger reformer, Mikhail Gorbachev, in 1985. His attempts to fix the economy would set the collapse in motion.

ПЕРЕСТРОЙКА
1985 – 1990

Glasnost and Perestroika

A younger leader set out to save the Soviet system by opening it up. His reforms released forces he could not control.

What Happened?

In March 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev (pictured) became General Secretary of the Communist Party. At 54, he was the youngest member of the Politburo. He believed the Soviet Union could survive only if it changed.

Gorbachev introduced two major policies. Glasnost (openness) allowed people to criticize the government, read banned books, and learn about crimes from the Soviet past. Perestroika (restructuring) tried to fix the economy by allowing some private businesses and giving factory managers more freedom.

  1. March 1985

    Gorbachev takes power after the death of Konstantin Chernenko.

  2. 1986 – 1987

    Glasnost and perestroika begin. Censorship eases and the government starts limited economic reforms.

  3. December 1987

    INF Treaty signed. Gorbachev and U.S. President Ronald Reagan agree to eliminate an entire class of nuclear missiles.

  4. March 1989

    First competitive elections. Voters choose a new Congress of People's Deputies, and some Communist Party candidates lose.

  5. March 1990

    The party's monopoly ends. The Communist Party gives up its guaranteed right to rule, and Gorbachev becomes President of the USSR.

Key Terms

Glasnostгласность
"Openness." Gorbachev's policy of allowing more freedom of speech and the press.
Perestroikaперестройка
"Restructuring." Gorbachev's attempt to reform the Soviet economy by adding some market features.
Politburo
The small group of top Communist Party leaders who made the most important decisions in the USSR.

What Role Did It Play in the Collapse?

Gorbachev's reforms were meant to save the Soviet system, but they weakened it instead. Glasnost worked quickly: once people could speak freely, they criticized the government, learned about Stalin's crimes, and organized national movements in the republics. Fear had held the system together, and glasnost removed it.

Perestroika failed. It broke down the old planned economy without building a working market to replace it, so shortages got worse, not better. People now had more freedom to complain and more to complain about.

АФГАНИСТАН
1979 – 1989

Invasion of Afghanistan

Soviet leaders expected a short operation. It became a ten-year war that drained the country's money and morale.

What Happened?

In December 1979, Soviet troops entered Afghanistan to prop up its struggling communist government. They seized the capital, Kabul, and installed a new leader loyal to Moscow.

Instead of a quick victory, the Soviets faced the mujahideen (pictured), Afghan guerrilla fighters who knew the mountains and had support from the United States, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and others. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers were killed. Afghan losses were far greater: historians estimate one to two million Afghans died, and millions more fled as refugees to Pakistan and Iran.

  1. December 1979

    Soviet troops invade. Special forces storm the presidential palace in Kabul.

  2. 1980

    The world responds. The United States and dozens of other countries boycott the Summer Olympics in Moscow.

  3. 1986

    Stinger missiles arrive. The U.S. supplies the mujahideen with shoulder-fired missiles that can shoot down Soviet helicopters. The same year, Gorbachev calls the war a "bleeding wound."

  4. April 1988

    The Geneva Accords. The USSR agrees to withdraw its troops.

  5. February 15, 1989

    The last Soviet troops leave Afghanistan.

Key Terms

Mujahideen
Afghan guerrilla fighters who resisted the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan.
Proxy war
A conflict where a major power supports one side instead of fighting directly, as the U.S. did by arming the mujahideen.
Guerrilla warfare
Fighting by small groups using surprise attacks rather than large battles.

What Role Did It Play in the Collapse?

The war cost money the struggling economy could not spare, and it cost thousands of young lives. Under glasnost, returning veterans and journalists described what the war was really like, and public support collapsed. Many Soviet citizens came to see it the way many Americans saw Vietnam.

The war also damaged the Red Army's reputation. A superpower had failed to defeat guerrilla fighters, and the withdrawal in 1989 signaled that Moscow was no longer willing to use force abroad. Months later, people across Eastern Europe would test that.

ЧЕРНОБЫЛЬ
April 26, 1986

Chernobyl Disaster

The worst nuclear accident in history, and a cover-up that taught Soviet citizens not to trust their government.

What Happened?

At 1:23 a.m. on April 26, 1986, Reactor No. 4 at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant (pictured) in Soviet Ukraine exploded during a safety test. A flawed reactor design and operator mistakes combined to blow the roof off the building and send radioactive material into the sky. Firefighters and plant workers rushed in without proper protection, and many died of radiation sickness in the weeks that followed.

Officials waited about a day and a half before evacuating the nearby city of Pripyat, home to roughly 49,000 people. The Soviet government said nothing publicly until a nuclear plant in Sweden detected radiation and demanded answers.

  1. April 26, 1986

    Reactor No. 4 explodes.

  2. April 27, 1986

    Pripyat is evacuated. Residents are told they will be gone for three days. They never return.

  3. April 28, 1986

    Sweden detects radiation. That evening, Soviet television reads a brief statement admitting an accident.

  4. May 14, 1986

    Gorbachev speaks to the nation about the disaster for the first time.

  5. November 1986

    The "sarcophagus" is finished. A concrete and steel shelter is built over the destroyed reactor.

Key Terms

Liquidators
The civilian and military workers sent to contain and clean up the Chernobyl disaster.
Exclusion zone
The area around Chernobyl, about 30 kilometers wide, closed to the public because of radiation.
Cover-up
An effort to hide the truth about a mistake or crime from the public.

What Role Did It Play in the Collapse?

Chernobyl showed Soviet citizens that their government would lie to them even when their lives were at risk. The cover-up destroyed trust in official news, and it pushed Gorbachev to expand glasnost so that problems could not be hidden as easily. Years later, he wrote that Chernobyl may have been the real cause of the Soviet Union's collapse.

The disaster also cost billions of rubles to clean up at a time when the economy was already struggling. In Ukraine and Belarus, anger over the disaster fed environmental protests that grew into movements for independence.

СВОБОДА
1989

Revolutions of 1989

When Gorbachev made clear the Soviet army would not step in, communist governments across Eastern Europe fell in a single year.

What Happened?

Click a numbered circle to learn about each revolution.

Key Terms

SolidaritySolidarność
A Polish trade union that became a mass movement against communist rule.
Sinatra Doctrine
Gorbachev's policy of letting Eastern European countries decide their own futures.
Satellite state
A country that is officially independent but controlled by a more powerful neighbor.

What Role Did It Play in the Collapse?

In a single year, the Soviet Union lost the ring of allied countries it had controlled since World War II. The Warsaw Pact military alliance and the Soviet-led trading bloc both broke up by mid-1991.

The revolutions also sent a message to people inside the Soviet Union. If Poland and Czechoslovakia could leave without Soviet tanks stopping them, then Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and other Soviet republics began asking why they could not leave too.

СТЕНА
November 9, 1989

Fall of the Berlin Wall

For 28 years, a wall split a city in two. It came down because of a mistake at a press conference.

What Happened?

After World War II, Germany was split into communist East Germany and democratic West Germany. The city of Berlin sat deep inside East Germany but was divided too. So many East Germans escaped through West Berlin that in August 1961 the East German government built a wall (pictured) around it overnight. At least 140 people were killed trying to cross it.

By the fall of 1989, East Germans were fleeing through Hungary and protesting by the hundreds of thousands at home. On November 9, party spokesman Günter Schabowski announced looser travel rules at a live press conference. When a reporter asked when they took effect, he looked at his notes and said, in effect, "immediately." Thousands of East Berliners (pictured) rushed to the border, and overwhelmed guards opened the gates.

  1. August 13, 1961

    The wall goes up. East German soldiers string barbed wire across the city overnight.

  2. June 12, 1987

    "Tear down this wall." U.S. President Ronald Reagan challenges Gorbachev in a speech at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.

  3. October 1989

    Mass protests in East Germany. Weekly marches in Leipzig grow to tens of thousands of people, and longtime leader Erich Honecker is forced out.

  4. November 9, 1989

    The border opens. East and West Berliners celebrate together on top of the wall.

  5. October 3, 1990

    Germany reunifies as a single democratic country.

Key Terms

East Germany
The German Democratic Republic (GDR), the communist state allied with the Soviet Union from 1949 to 1990.
Checkpoint
A guarded crossing point in the wall, such as Checkpoint Charlie.
Reunification
The joining of East and West Germany into one country in 1990.

What Role Did It Play in the Collapse?

The Berlin Wall was the most famous symbol of the Cold War divide. When it fell and the Soviet Union did nothing to stop it, the whole world saw that Soviet power in Europe was finished.

Germany reunified less than a year later as a member of NATO, the Western military alliance, and Soviet troops began leaving the country. Communist hardliners in Moscow saw this as a humiliating defeat, and their anger helped drive the coup attempt of 1991.

ПУТЧ
August 19 – 21, 1991

The 1991 Coup Attempt

Hardliners tried to save the Soviet Union by force. Their failure destroyed it in four months.

What Happened?

By 1991, many of the fifteen Soviet republics, led by Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, were demanding independence. Gorbachev negotiated a New Union Treaty that would give the republics much more power. It was scheduled to be signed on August 20, 1991.

The day before the signing, a group of Communist hardliners, including the heads of the KGB and the army, placed Gorbachev under house arrest at his vacation home in Crimea. Tanks rolled into Moscow. Boris Yeltsin (pictured), the recently elected President of Russia, climbed onto a tank outside the Russian parliament building and called on people to resist. Tens of thousands of citizens surrounded the building, and many soldiers refused to attack them. Within three days, the coup had collapsed.

  1. August 19, 1991

    The coup begins. Gorbachev is placed under house arrest, and state television plays the ballet Swan Lake on repeat.

  2. August 21, 1991

    The coup fails. Three young men are killed in clashes with armored vehicles. The plotters give up, and Gorbachev returns to Moscow.

  3. August 24, 1991

    Ukraine declares independence. Voters confirm it by a huge majority in December.

  4. December 8, 1991

    The Belovezha Accords. Leaders of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus declare that the USSR no longer exists and form the Commonwealth of Independent States.

  5. December 25 – 26, 1991

    The end. Gorbachev resigns, the Soviet flag is lowered over the Kremlin, and the Soviet Union is formally dissolved.

Key Terms

Coupпутч
A sudden, illegal attempt to seize control of a government, often by military or security forces.
KGB
The Soviet secret police and intelligence agency.
Commonwealth of Independent States
A loose association of former Soviet republics formed in December 1991.

What Role Did It Play in the Collapse?

The coup was meant to save the Soviet Union, but it destroyed it. The plotters had tried to use the army and the KGB to hold the country together, and they failed in public, in front of the whole world. The Communist Party was disgraced, and Yeltsin banned its activities in Russia.

Gorbachev came back from house arrest with almost no authority left. Yeltsin, who had stood on the tank, now held the real power. In the weeks after the coup, republic after republic declared independence, and four months later the Soviet Union no longer existed.

РАСПАД
1990 – 1991

The Final Collapse

One by one, the republics declared independence. By the end of 1991, the Soviet Union was gone.
